tier_reason: notes.txt has only approximate '~NN us' dev-log figures and no raw benchmark output. The benchmark code (benchmark.cpp) and the Makefile compilers and flags are public, but the 5950X is named only for the earlier perf-stat section, and the notes never say which CPU or which build (g++-12 or clang-stage2 .so) produced the microsecond figures, so this is first-party evidence short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: notes.txt (author's dev log, approximate '~' figures): on the nonkeywords corpus, pht with the icrc32 hasher and --string-compare=check1memcmp (~69 us) beats gperf default (~95 us) [~1.38x, derived from page data]. On the mixed corpus, the same pht config (~152 us) beats gperf default (~188 us) [~1.24x, derived from page data], and beats gperf's best mixed config, --inline-strings (~184 us) [~1.21x, derived from page data]. With --string-compare=memcmp, gperf beats every one of the author's hash variants on all three corpora. The keywords-only corpus has no numbers: gperf beats all memcmp variants, and icrc32 with check1memcmp is only 'competitive' with gperf, so pht does NOT win that workload. frozen::unordered_map with lehmer128 is ~85 us (nonkeywords) and ~209 us (mixed), slower than the icrc32/check1memcmp pht in both [derived from page data].
corrections.workload: Google Benchmark loop (benchmark.cpp) looks up every identifier token in three corpora. map-to-tokens.cpp builds the corpora from jquery-3.5.1.js: keywords-only, non-keywords-only, and mixed, whitespace-padded to ~287 KB each. Lookups run against the JavaScript keyword set (token.gperf). Each implementation is compiled as a shared library and loaded with dlopen: dozens of generated pht variants, gperf 3.1 option combos, mygperf, bsearch and linear scans, frozen::unordered_map, std::unordered_map, and Rust phf and std::collections::HashMap.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Makefile: on Linux, CXX=g++-12, and every implementation is also built with ~/Toolchains/clang-stage2/bin/clang++ (-clang.so variants). Flags are -std=c++20 -g -O3 -fvisibility=hidden -fPIC, plus -fcf-protection=full -msse4 -maes on Linux only; the benchmark binary adds -fno-lto. On macOS (aarch64), the Makefile does not set CXX (make default) and uses Homebrew google-benchmark 1.7.1. The baseline is gperf 3.1 (per the generated/gperf_.cpp header). notes.txt does not say which compiler build produced the quoted figures.
corrections.hardware: notes.txt says 'my 5950X' (AMD Ryzen 9 5950X) only for the perf-stat branch-miss section. The microsecond figures carry no CPU statement. The icrc32 pht configs are only built on Linux x86 (Intel CRC32 intrinsic, Linux-only block in the Makefile). This is consistent with the 5950X, but the file does not say so.
corrections.caveats: Tier C, not A. notes.txt is a free-text dev log with rounded '~' microsecond figures; the repo has no committed results file or raw Google Benchmark output. The CPU (5950X) is stated only for the perf-stat section, and the notes never say whether the g++-12 or the clang (-clang.so) build produced the quoted figures. The win depends on the workload. pht icrc32+check1memcmp beats gperf 3.1 default on the nonkeywords (~1.38x) and mixed (~1.24x) corpora. On keywords-only it only ties gperf ('competitive'). Every pht variant with --string-compare=memcmp loses to gperf on all three corpora. --string-compare is an option of the author's generators (generate-pht.cpp, generate-mygperf.py), not of gperf. The harness also builds std::unordered_map, frozen::unordered_map, Rust phf and Rust std HashMap variants, but notes.txt publishes no std::unordered_map or Rust numbers. The corpora are synthetic: map-to-tokens.cpp filters identifiers from jquery-3.5.1.js. LICENSE is CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0: GitHub reports NOASSERTION, and the LICENSE text confirms it. README says 'EDUCATIONAL USE ONLY', so usability is 'reference': no copying and no patent grant. There are no commits since 2023-03-12 (more than 3 years); the repo is not archived. The companion talk (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DMQ_HcNSOAI, 'Faster than Rust and C++: the PERFECT hash table', title confirmed via YouTube oEmbed) could not be read, so any speedup figures stated in the talk are not reflected here. The record also says the technique was reimplemented in private:developer-source (fastcpp::phf). The verifier did not check that repo, and it is not evidence for this repo's numbers.

notes: The notes.txt numbers match the record, but the original claimed_speedup misread the keywords line: '--string-compare=check1memcmp' is an option of the pht/mygperf generators, not of gperf. claimed_speedup is corrected. The metadata checks out: 226 stars, last commit 2023-03-12, CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0, not a fork, not archived. compared_against_cpp_std_directly stays true because the harness includes std-unordered-map.cpp, but no std::unordered_map numbers are published.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The README table (added in commit e4acd52a, 2016-10-06) is the output of the author's benchmark repo github.com/julian-klode/hashbench (bench-runner.c, Makefile, render-results.py), which the 2016 announcement post links. That repo states the compiler (gcc via $(CROSS)-gcc) and flags (-O2 -g -fPIE -fstack-protector-strong, --static; gperf --pic --readonly-tables), and the README gives the jak-x230 CPU (Core i5-3320M). A covers only the jak-x230 column, and the gcc version is not stated.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README Performance table (GB/s, higher is better). On jak-x230 (amd64, Core i5-3320M), Trie is 2.4 vs gperf 1.3 case-sensitive [~1.85x, derived from page data], and Trie (*) is 2.2 vs gperf (*) 0.7 case-insensitive [~3.1x, derived from page data]. Comparing like with like across all 7 host/arch columns, Trie is ~1.85x (x230) to ~5x (plummer ppc64el, 2.0 vs 0.4) faster than gperf case-sensitive. Trie (*) is ~2x (eller mipsel, 0.2 vs 0.1, coarsely rounded) to ~4x (asachi arm64, 0.8 vs 0.2) faster than gperf (*) case-insensitive [derived from page data].
corrections.workload: Each of the 82 field names from Debian Packages/Sources files is hashed 1,000,000 times back-to-back. hashbench also probes 3 extra words: Hallo, PaCKage, PackageXXX. Throughput is the summed word bytes divided by the total ns, reported in GB/s. The table has 7 host/arch columns on 5 hosts: jak-x230 and backup (amd64), asachi.d.o (arm64/armel/armhf), plummer.d.o (ppc64el), and eller.d.o (mipsel). Other competitors are re2c, djb hash variants, and APT's AlphaHash.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Per the julian-klode/hashbench Makefile: gcc (CC := $(CROSS)-gcc; version not stated). CFLAGS ?= -O2 -g -fPIE -fstack-protector-strong -Wformat -Werror=format-security, and LDFLAGS ?= --static. The gperf baseline is generated with `gperf --includes --pic --readonly-tables`, plus --ignore-case for gperf (*). The README notes also point to gcc bug 77729 (extra zero-extend instructions).
corrections.hardware: jak-x230: Intel Core i5-3320M (stated in the README legend). backup (amd64) and the Debian porterboxes asachi.debian.org (arm64/armel/armhf), plummer.debian.org (ppc64el) and eller.debian.org (mipsel) are named by hostname only, with no CPU model. The legend's 'barriere has an Opteron 23xx' refers to an earlier table; barriere is not in the current table.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark code is not in the triehash repo. It lives in github.com/julian-klode/hashbench (MIT, 0 stars, last commit 2016-10-06), which the author's 2016-09-25 blog post links. Its Makefile and render-results.py produce exactly the README table layout, and the table landed in triehash the same day (2016-10-06). The gcc version is not stated. Only jak-x230 (Core i5-3320M) has a CPU model; the other hosts are named by hostname only. The method favors branchy switch-based code: each word is hashed 1,000,000 times in a row, so the branch predictor is fully trained and the cache is hot. The gperf baseline was generated with --pic --readonly-tables rather than gperf defaults. The mipsel figures (0.1-0.2 GB/s) are too coarsely rounded for meaningful ratios. The numbers date from 2016. re2c matchers and APT's unrolled AlphaHash (apt (**), 2.3 GB/s on x230) also come close to Trie. triehash is a Perl script (GitHub language: Shell) that generates C code, and the generated C is directly callable from C++. The last commit on main is 2019-04-16; the debian/master packaging branch has commits up to 2022-12-14. Both are more than 3 years old, so the project is abandoned. APT uses triehash: apt-pkg/CMakeLists.txt runs it with --ignore-case to generate tagfile-keys (verified on the Debian/apt GitHub mirror).

notes: Upgraded to A after finding the linked benchmark repo (julian-klode/hashbench), which states the compiler and flags. The original '1.8-3.4x' range understated the gap across architectures and paired case-sensitive Trie with case-insensitive gperf. It is corrected to like-for-like ratios: ~1.85-5x case-sensitive and ~2-4x case-insensitive. The metadata checks out: MIT, 49 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit on main 2019-04-16, used in APT.
